We trained a reinforcement-learning dispatcher and gave it every advantage: the same shortlist of candidate tasks, the same 24 measurements per task, the same routing, pickers and battery machinery. Only the choice was learned. It improved steadily while training, finished ahead of the built-in dispatcher and level with the urgency rule — and still lost to the hand-built rules by 5.3%. Given identical information, there was no headroom left for it to find. (Caveat: a modest training budget with a simple algorithm; a much larger tuned run might close that gap.)

+22% over the built-in dispatcher on wave days, +49% on live-stream days (both far past the ±certain mark: t = 9.3 and 12.2 across 144 paired days). Those are for the full shipped fleet — the rules together with the self-tuner, which is what actually runs. Earlier versions of this page quoted the rules with the tuner switched off (+21% / +47%), which understated the system by up to five points under spills; the tuner is part of the machine, not an optional extra. These are the 2026-09-06 re-measurement: the earlier table had been produced before a simulator change and never re-run, which left the live-stream absolutes 40–55 points low. Wave was unaffected, and the margin barely moved (+48.9% → +47.5%, both for the tuner-off arm) because it is a paired comparison — but the numbers were wrong for twelve days, and re-running the benchmark on every simulator change is now the rule. The safety columns matter as much as the value: across all 1,152 runs our controllers stranded zero robots, while the baselines repeatedly wedge robots holding pods. The self-tuner adds +0.5% on wave (statistically real, t = 2.4) and +0.9% on stream (t = 1.1 — below the bar).

One fix — a robot’s direct look now replaces what the map believed instead of casting one vote against old history — and it carries through either brain. 9 · How to read those three charts

The map never says “blocked” or “clear”. For every cell, on every step, it commits to a number between 0 and 1: how likely it thinks that square is blocked right now. Grading numbers like that is a different job from grading a router, and it is the job these three panels do — over 4.8 million predictions per map, one for every highway cell on every step of 24 days.

What a is. Take one prediction, square how far it landed from what actually happened, and average that over every prediction ever made. Say 0.9 on a cell that really is blocked and you are charged (1 − 0.9)² = 0.01. Say 0.9 on a cell that is clean and you are charged 0.81. Confident and right is nearly free; confident and wrong is ruinous; hedging at 0.5 costs 0.25 every single time, whatever happens. Lower is better and 0 is perfect. The shipped map scores 0.0204, the old one 0.0310.

Why that number on its own means nothing — and what “skill” fixes. Only 3.2% of cells are blocked at any moment. So a lazy map that ignores its eyes entirely and answers “3.2%” on every cell forever already scores 0.031 — it looks almost as good as the real thing, purely because blockages are rare. Skill strips that out: it is the fraction of the lazy map’s error you actually remove. 0.0 means you have matched a forecaster that never looked; 1.0 would be perfect. The shipped map scores +0.351. The old map scored +0.013 — which is the uncomfortable finding hiding in this figure: as a thing to route on it was clearly useful, but as a forecaster it was almost indistinguishable from a fleet that had never opened its eyes.

Left — precision and recall
Pick how sure the map must be before you act as though a cell is blocked, and you get one pair of numbers: recall, the share of genuinely blocked cells you flag, and precision, the share of your flags that are real. Slide that bar from paranoid to trusting and the pairs trace the curve. The flat dashed line is random guessing, which sits at 3.2% because that is how rare blockages are. The shipped map holds high precision out to about 85% recall — it can name almost every blocked cell without inventing ones that aren’t. Area under the curve: 0.367 shipped, 0.260 old, 0.032 random.
Middle — is it honest?
Gather every prediction where the map said “about 70%” and ask what fraction of those cells really were blocked. Plot claimed against observed. Landing on the dashed diagonal means the map’s confidence can be taken at face value. Its beliefs are near-binary — nearly all the mass sits at the two ends — and that is exactly where it lands on the line: says 98.0%, is 97.9%. The sag in the middle is the one deliberate exception: a cell nobody has looked at recently is parked at 50% by convention, and such cells are almost never actually blocked. Replacing that convention with the true base rate was tried and rejected, because it rebuilds the mountain of stale “probably clean” history that the overwrite rule exists to demolish.
Right — and the punchline
Steps between a spill appearing and the fleet believing in it; each curve climbs to the fraction of spills detected by then. The two curves lie on top of each other — median 1–2 steps for both maps. That is the most informative thing in the whole figure, because it rules out the obvious explanation. The fix was never about noticing sooner: both maps saw every spill immediately. The old one then let a few steps of stale “clean” votes outvote the fresh sighting and forget what it had just seen; the new one keeps believing until someone actually looks again. Two identical lines are the proof that sustaining a belief, not acquiring it, is worth the entire +28.8 value difference.

Taken together the three panels answer three questions that are easy to confuse: does it discriminate? (left — yes, 11× random), can its numbers be believed as numbers? (middle — yes, to a tenth of a point where it acts), and where did the improvement come from? (right — memory, not perception). A map can pass any one of these and fail the others; the old map passed the third and failed the first two.

The full keep/cut ledger for all 32 mechanisms now lives in its own Ablation tab.

“Rollout” means two different things here — one is our biggest win, the other is our cleanest failure. We name them: the board rollout (imagine the future of pieces already on the board) and the crystal-ball rollout (imagine pieces that haven’t arrived yet). Chess-thinking vs fortune-telling.

The BOARD ROLLOUT — imagining how current work plays out (the win)

When a robot must choose between tasks that already exist, the controller plays each choice forward in its head: drive there, meet the picker, queue at the station, deliver — and picks the choice whose imagined future scores best. This is the rollout that beat the simple “grab the closest/most urgent task” baseline: switching it off costs −7.2% of a day’s value, the single largest mechanism effect we ever measured. The self-tuner is the same idea one level up: it copies the whole warehouse and imagines the next 100 steps under different settings. Both imaginations are about things that are real right now.

The CRYSTAL-BALL ROLLOUT — feeding predicted future orders into that imagination (the failure)

The tempting upgrade: also show the imagination orders that haven’t arrived yet (“at 2pm, rack 31 will get an order”). We tested this with a cheat that skips every prediction problem: the controller was handed the actual future, perfectly. Result, on steady demand:

how far ahead it could seeeffect on the day
10 steps±0 (nothing)
25 steps−1.7
100 steps−5.3
the whole day−11.2 (−3.4%, certain)

The more future it saw, the worse it did. Perfect knowledge — so no forecast, however clever, can do better than this ceiling. That is why we never built a demand predictor.

Why knowing the future HURTS on steady demand

Because knowing an order early doesn’t let you serve it early — an order can’t be picked before it exists. So the future knowledge has no product to sell. But it still has a cost: the imagination starts favoring choices that “set up” future orders — passing over genuinely urgent work in front of it to prepare for work that cannot be touched yet. Like a waiter who knows tomorrow’s reservations perfectly and starts rearranging tonight’s tables for them: the future can’t be served yet, so every present action taken for it is pure cost. The damage growing steadily with how far it looks (the table above) is the fingerprint of exactly this mechanism.

Why it’s merely USELESS (not harmful) when demand shifts

One objection remained: our demand was steady — the popular racks never moved, so of course preparing was pointless. We answered it with real data: grocery-order patterns from a real dataset (3,200+ orders) show demand genuinely drifts through the day — produce peaks mid-morning, snacks mid-afternoon, zone shares swinging 11–17%. We built that drift into the warehouse and re-ran the perfect-knowledge test: flat (first seed batch leaned +4.6, a twice-as-large fresh batch flipped it to −5.3; combined ≈ 0). Why flat instead of harmful? Under drift, leaning toward where demand is heading finally has a small real benefit — but it only roughly cancels the setting-up-the-future tax. And why no better than flat: robots re-chase demand every time they finish a task (~25 steps), while real demand needs 100+ steps to move its hotspot meaningfully. The fleet never falls behind, so prediction has nothing to fix. A dog on a leash doesn’t need to predict a slow walker’s route.

The one prediction that DOES pay

Contrast with the spill result on the Scoreboard: predicting that a seen spill is still there is worth real value (+12.8, and 76% of all sensing value with weak sensors). The difference: a spill’s persistence is knowledge you can act on now (route around it), while a future order is knowledge you can only act on when it arrives anyway. Prediction pays when the present can use it — never when only the future can.

What these measures actually mean, and how to read the three curves they come from, is explained under Scoreboard → “How to read those three charts”. One honest note on specificity. The target we set ourselves was 90% on both sensitivity and specificity. Specificity comes in at 99.87% — but that is the easy half, and we would rather say so than bank it: only 3.2% of cells are ever blocked, so a map that simply answered “clear” everywhere would score 100% specificity and 0% sensitivity. The half that actually binds is sensitivity, and that is the one physics caps at 84.9%.

That is the right shape for a safety setting, and it is the new default.

how good could the self-tuner possibly be? (stress days, 48 paired)valuevs fixedstranded
shipped fixed settings742.3—123
the best single constant we found (“be 20% more cautious about battery”)808.2+65.969
the self-tuner as shipped799.9+57.695
a mind-reader picking the best settings for each day—+147.1—

The most uncomfortable number in this project, and we went looking for it on purpose. Every mechanism we wanted to reject was tested against a mind-reader. The self-tuner — the one we wanted to keep — never was. So we measured it.

It captures 39% of what a mind-reader picking one setting per day would get. And against something you could actually ship, it is a tie: one fixed constant scores +65.9 against the tuner’s +57.6, and head-to-head that difference is a coin flip (the constant wins 24 days out of 48). So the tuner’s whole benefit here is reproducible by changing one number — it is finding that number rather than beating it. That is honestly what a tuner should do when the right answer is a constant, and it found it without being told. But it means “+1% a day” is not evidence that adapting is what pays.

Where the real headroom is: a constant gets +65.9, a per-day mind-reader gets +147.1. That gap cannot be closed by any fixed setting, and the tuner does not close it either. Read alongside the charging result — the same trick worth +91 on a hard day and −4 on an easy one — the picture is consistent: this warehouse wants different settings on different days, that is worth more than any single answer, and we have not built the thing that captures it.

do the different kinds of knowledge add up? (48 days, spills on)valuevs normal
the shipped fleet755.6—
+ knows every future order735.6−19.9
+ knows every spill in advance785.5+30.0
+ knows both792.7+37.2

The last open objection to the “don’t predict” result was that we only ever tested one kind of knowledge at a time — maybe knowing the future orders only helps if you also know where the floor will be blocked. Run together, the two barely interact (+27 more than the sum of the parts, but not statistically solid at this sample size). The don’t-predict finding survives being tested jointly. Knowing about spills is worth real value, as it always has been — that is knowledge about something that already exists.

6 · Does knowing the future ever pay?

six independent tests, all no

The charging test is the sharpest of the six: a deliberately wrong forecast beat the true one, and a constant threshold at the same average was worth nothing (+0.3%). So the gain there is not information at all — it is that moving the threshold triggers extra top-ups, because raising a threshold causes a charge while lowering one merely postpones.

…and what happened when we built it

48 paired days per column
charge threshold rulestress daysordinary daysrobots stranded (stress)
fixed at 0.40 (shipped)742.31052.4123
oscillate ±0.10, no forecast at all805.5 (+63.2)1039.1 (−13.2)80
the self-tuner (picks a level)799.9 (+57.6)1061.2 (+8.9)95
self-tuner + oscillation833.5 (+91.2)1048.7 (−3.7)93

Two surprises. A one-line rule that just alternates a number, with no information in it whatsoever, matches the entire self-tuner on stress days — a controller that copies the whole warehouse every 50 steps and plays out candidate settings 100 steps ahead. Its average threshold is identical to the fixed rule, so the gain is the movement and nothing else. And it stacks: adding it to the tuner is worth another +33.6. Then the ordinary-day check refused it. On a normal day nothing strands in any arm, so the safety it buys is worthless and the extra charging trips are pure cost — it goes mildly negative, and it wipes out the tuner’s own edge. The same mechanism is worth +91 on a hard day and −4 on an easy one. So it never becomes a default; it becomes a move the tuner can audition, adopted only where it pays. Which is the best argument yet for having a self-tuner at all: no single constant is right for both days, and the tuner doesn’t need one to be.

8 · Known open items

stated, not hidden
itemstatus
Two robots park forever on one live-stream dayCause confirmed; the fix costs 8.1%, so it stays open. 17 empty racks (10% of the floor) close it completely — 2 wedged robots to 0 over 144 days — but cost −48.5 on-time value (t = −4.91), because an empty rack is a pod not earning. Free on quiet days, where the wedges are; −9.6% on busy days, where they never happen. Earlier notes on this item said the wedge merely relocated: that came from testing 3 and 9 empty racks, which is too little slack to test the hypothesis at all. Superseded detail: We found a real bug on the way: the floor grid was rebuilt from scratch every step, quietly putting back the pods we thought we had removed from the charging bays — so the warehouse was running 180 pods for 172 places to put them, eight worse than the “no spare slots” we had diagnosed. Correcting it does fix day 125 — and breaks day 106, which used to be clean. Adding genuinely empty slots (3, then 9) changes neither. Two wedged robots in 48 days before, two after, on a different day: the fix relocated the failure instead of removing it, the fourth time that has happened here. And it does not ship, for a sharper reason: with the bay pods really gone, the built-in dispatcher starts parking pods on the charging bays (it has no notion of keep-out, our controller does) and loses 39 points — which would have widened our headline margin from +62.6% to +80.7% purely by making the opponent worse. The pod on the bay turned out to be load-bearing. So: bug documented, fix measured and shelved, item open.
Threshold movement as a charging tacticBuilt 2026-09-06. +91.2 with the tuner on stress days (t = 3.81), −3.7 on ordinary days. Gated, not shipped as a default — it belongs in the tuner’s move set. See the charging section.

Everything we built — kept or cut

The rule was set in advance: a mechanism ships only if it is worth at least 3% on paired days, judged on the same warehouses and the same orders. Safety mechanisms are judged on stranded and collision counts instead. Eight kept, twenty-two cut — plus two more that ship on safety alone and make no value claim (the value-rate picker sequencing, folded into the rollout ablation, and the charging bays), which is why the full ledger in the paper counts ten kept.

Read the two halves together and the pattern is hard to miss: everything kept reasons about things that already exist — the tasks in hand, the batteries draining, the spill somebody saw. Everything cut tried to act on something that did not exist yet, or on a guess no observation had confirmed.

What we set out to test

Whether a warehouse can be run well by a controller that imagines consequences using known physics — no black boxes — and how close that gets to a system with perfect information. Three questions: does imagining beat reacting, does honest sensing beat ignorance, and can the fleet safely manage its own batteries?

The pattern underneath

One sentence covers every row above: imagine the future of what exists; never the existence of what doesn’t. Predicting that a spill you saw is still there is worth real money (+12.8 value, and 76% of all sensing value when sensors are weak). Predicting where the next order will land is worth nothing or less — and not because it is hard: the planner was handed perfect knowledge of future orders and still lost. A warehouse can act on the present and can only wait for the future.

The second lesson was about honest belief. Most of the gap between our fleet and an omniscient one turned out to be a bad update rule rather than weak sensors: the map let a hundred stale “this cell was clean” observations outvote a robot’s fresh sighting. Letting one direct look overwrite the memory recovered nearly the whole gap (+28.8 value, spill collisions cut to a third) and made the map’s stated confidence match reality to a tenth of a percentage point.

Honest limitations

  • Everything here is simulation. No physical robot has been driven, and battery timescales are compressed so that charging decisions fit inside a 500-step day.
  • The headline benchmark table is one floor plan and one fleet size; scale evidence comes from a separate 46-configuration campaign, not from these runs.
  • Baselines are strong heuristics we implemented, plus a reinforcement-learning dispatcher we trained ourselves (it landed 5.3% below the champion, above the built-in dispatcher). These are not published reinforcement-learning results, and our learner had a modest budget — a large tuned run remains untested.
  • The self-tuner’s benefit is modest and conditional: real where charging binds, and zero once spills make its imagined futures noisy.
  • Known loose end: one live-stream day (seed 125) ends with two robots still holding pods; 574 of 576 runs are clean.

Every criterion this project set itself — and whether it was met

These are not criteria invented afterwards. Each one was written down in the proposal, the roadmap’s per-milestone “done-when”, or the standing deliverables list before the work that would satisfy it. Two of them turned out to be impossible; where that happened it is said plainly rather than quietly dropped.

60met
0partly met
5not met
0impossible
92%of 65 criteria

64 criteria, and nothing on this list is impossible. That is a change. Two targets were recorded for months as physically unreachable; on 2026-09-06 — reading the original proposal against the results, rather than the roadmap against the results — both turned out to have been scored against the wrong measurement, and both pass. Two further criteria surfaced in the same pass that had never been measured at all: one passes by 800×, one fails by 10×.

The five that remain are one target that turns out to be unreachable and where we sit within 5% of the physical ceiling (phantom hard-blocks), one bug whose cause is now known and whose cheapest fix costs 8% (the wedged robots), two builds deliberately not attempted, and one opportunity nobody asked for — it exists only because we measured the self-tuner’s own ceiling on the final day. None is blocked, and only one of the five was ever something the original proposal actually asked for.

Worth separating, because they get confused. Of these 65 criteria, the great majority come from the original written proposal. A handful were added later by us — bars we set ourselves while chasing problems, which are stricter than anything we promised. And one appeared on the final day because we went looking for a ceiling nobody had asked for. Failing a bar you invented for yourself is a different kind of thing from failing one you promised, and the rows below do not currently distinguish them.

3 · Making the spill map act

3 met, 1 partly, 1 impossible
statuscriterionevidence, or why not
METWith-map vs without-map, under spillsthe centrepiece: 800.6 → 850.1, collisions 364 → 80, and the phase boundary mapped at both ends
METSensitivity ≥ 90%92.2% — 424 of 460 real spills detected. We had this scored wrong for months. The proposal asks what share of spills get caught; we had been reporting what share of blocked squares get caught at every instant (84.76%), which is a far harsher question, and calling the target physically impossible on that basis. Both numbers are real, they just answer different questions, and the target was written about the first one. Corrected 2026-09-06 by reading the proposal against the results instead of the other way round.
METSpecificity ≥ 90%99.87%, measured 2026-09-06 (3,358 false flags in 2.55M checks). Reported with a caveat rather than as a win: at a 3.2% base rate this is the easy half — a map answering “clear” everywhere scores 100%.
METMedian detection latency ≤ 15 steps2 steps. The proposal says median; we had been marking this half-failed on the mean (20.4), which a handful of spills nobody drives past for a long time drags upward. Same slip as the row above, corrected the same day.
METCalibration within ±10%says 98.0%, is 97.9% — honest to a tenth of a point where it acts
NOT MET≤ 1 phantom hard-block per 1,000 steps9.8 per 1,000 — missed by ten times. But a mind-reader misses it by nine. A phantom hard-block is a square the robots refuse to drive through that is actually perfectly clear. It costs detours, not crashes. Having just been caught calling one target impossible without checking, we checked this one: a perfect-memory oracle, fed exactly the same glimpses the real fleet gets, scores 9.2 against our 9.8. We are within 5% of the best any map with these eyes could do, and the best is still nine times over budget. The reason is not obvious and is worth keeping: with a perfect sensor a phantom is never a wrong sighting, it is an old one. A robot saw a spill, the cleaner mopped it, and nobody has walked past since. A mind-reader with perfect recall is blind in exactly the same way, because the missing information was never observed by anyone. The only cure is looking more often. This target was written for a warehouse with denser sensing than ours; no amount of cleverness in the inference can substitute. And we are not fixing it, for two reasons we checked rather than assumed. First, it is close enough — within 5% of anything’s best. Second, we tried the obvious fix and it does nothing. These phantoms are memories, not mistakes, so the natural cure is to make the map let go of old sightings; there was even a neat structural reason to expect that to work, because beliefs used to fade toward exactly the threshold and so could never quite drop below it. We made that adjustable and pushed it to the extreme. Phantoms went 7.2 to 7.1 per thousand. Nothing else moved either. The reason is a second number we had not accounted for: one clear look writes such strong evidence that it takes 263 steps to fade regardless, and somebody almost always drives past long before then. Which means we have not shown a trade-off between phantoms and spotting real spills — we have shown the cheap dial is simply inert.
META decision takes under 1 second (5 robots)1.3 ms typical, 510 ms at the very worst across 3,992 decisions — roughly 800× inside budget. Also never measured before today. One caveat reported rather than hidden: the very first decision after starting the program takes 1–1.7 s, which is loading code and warming caches, not thinking. A real deployment pays that once at boot.

The recorded cause was “no spare storage slots”, and it is correct — but proving it took a proper sweep. Small amounts of slack (3 then 9 empty racks) do nothing, which had us briefly concluding the hypothesis was wrong. At 17 empty racks the wedge closes completely, 2 wedged robots to 0 across 144 days. It is a storage problem after all. And the cure costs 8.1% of everything delivered (−48.5, t = −4.91) — an empty rack is a pod that is not earning. Against a bar of +3%, that is not close. The split is the interesting part: on busy days the slack costs 9.6% and there was never a wedge to prevent; on quiet days it is free and that is where both wedges live. Slack wants to be something the warehouse varies by the hour, not a constant — but we have not built that, so we are not claiming it. Also found along the way: a real bug (the floor was carrying eight more pods than places to put them, because a documented rule had never actually executed), whose fix is separately unshippable because it costs the built-in dispatcher 39 points it has no way to avoid.
NOT METProve the dispatch rules work outside our own simulatorScoped, not built. Our liveness rules live as flags inside our own fork, so the rules and the world they were tuned on are the same codebase — a fair reviewer can ask whether the +6.8% is a property of the warehouse or of our copy of it. The check is to re-implement them as an adapter over the untouched borrowed simulator and see the gain reproduce. It has to be an adapter, never a patch: the entire value of the head-to-head rests on the opponent being unmodified. That is a multi-hour build whose failure mode is a subtly different environment that silently invalidates the comparison, so it wants a fresh session and a parity check, not the tail end of a long one.
NOT METCapture the per-day settings headroomNot a criterion anyone wrote down — it only exists because we went looking for the self-tuner’s ceiling on the last day, and it is now the biggest open opportunity in the project. A mind-reader choosing the best settings for each individual day scores +147. The best single setting you could actually ship scores +66. The self-tuner scores +58 — which means it captures 39% of the ceiling, and, more awkwardly, ties that one fixed setting head-to-head (it wins 24 days out of 48: a coin flip). So the tuner is finding a good constant rather than beating one. The 2.2× gap between a constant and a per-day choice is real, unreachable by any fixed number, and unclaimed by anything built here. The charging result points the same way: one trick worth +91 on a hard day and −4 on an easy one. The warehouse wants different settings on different days and nothing we built captures that.
NOT METLet an idle picker step out of an AGV’s wayDeliberately not attempted. A picker standing idle in an aisle can block a robot that needs to pass. Every liveness rule that shipped works by vetoing a move an agent already asked to make; this one is the first that would have to invent a move for an agent that asked for nothing — writing into the referee’s internal path and action state rather than filtering it. That is a riskier class of change, and the prize is small: the worst case it targets is a single 92-step wait across 144 days. This project’s own rule is that at that rarity a fix has to be worth more than the cost of re-verifying everything it perturbs, and by that rule it does not yet qualify.

The two targets we thought were impossible

and were not — why the correction matters more than the pass

For most of this project two targets were written up as unreachable: 90% of spills detected, and detection latency under 15 steps. The reasoning looked sound — robots only see what they drive past, so given where they actually drove the best any map could do is 84.9%, and we sit at 84.76%, or 99.8% of that. All of that is still true. It just does not answer the question the proposal asked. The proposal asks what fraction of spills the map catches, not what fraction of blocked squares it is holding at any instant; on spills the map catches 92.2%. And it asks for a median latency, which is 2 steps, not the mean, which is 20.

Both pass. But the useful part is not the pass — it is that a project can carry a false failure for months while measuring diligently the whole time, because the number was compared against the wrong definition and nobody re-read the original document. The same pass turned up two criteria that had never been measured at all. Read the requirements against the results, not the plan against the results.

Full detail on any row lives in the All numbers tab, the Ablation ledger, or docs/NOTES.md in the repository, which records every experiment including the ones that failed.

What is this?

This page is a window into a simulated robot warehouse. Robot carts called carry shelf towers () full of products to , where grab the items customers ordered. Every order is worth points, but only if it arrives before its — late deliveries score zero. The warehouse’s score for a day is its .

What’s a “day”?

One run is 500 — about nine minutes of simulated time. Each numbered has its own pre-made list of orders, so two controllers can be tested on the exact same day and compared fairly. Robots also have batteries: real ones last hours, but we use so charging actually matters inside one run. A robot that hits empty away from a bay is — our safety rule is that this must never happen.

Standard vs the self-tuning controller

Both controllers use the same brain for choosing tasks. The difference is three charging habits: the battery , the safety margin, and the . The standard controller keeps those numbers fixed all day. The self-tuning controller () pauses every 50 steps, makes a in memory, plays 100 steps of the future in that copy under a few different settings, and keeps whichever setting ended with the best score.

Why this is a world model (really)

A is a model of how the world changes that lives inside the decision-maker and is used to imagine “what would happen if I did X?” before doing it — and the decision is then made from those imagined futures. That is a specific, checkable claim, and this system meets it three ways:

1. The controller carries a prediction machine. The self-tuning loop above is not a metaphor: every 50 steps the controller builds a in its own memory and plays 100 steps of the future in it under each candidate setting. No idea is ever tested on the real warehouse — it is tested in the controller’s imagination first, and only the winner touches reality. That imagine→score→act loop is the defining behavior of model-based control, as opposed to trial and error.

2. It imagines from what the robots know, not from the answer key. On live-stream days the copy contains only the orders the fleet has actually seen — the model rolls the future forward from the fleet’s knowledge, not from ground truth. And for spills, the fleet keeps a : its own internal, sometimes-wrong picture of where hazards are, built from sightings and corrected by experience. Predicting from your own beliefs is exactly what separates a world model from cheating by peeking — and we measured it: the honest version scores higher than injecting guessed futures.

3. The model has to be right, or it loses. This isn’t decoration: when we tried a hand-guessed model of traffic clashes, every variant lost value; replacing the guess with the simulated model flipped the sign and got shipped. The predictions are load-bearing.

One honest boundary: the physics rules inside the model are written down, not learned by a neural network (unlike Dreamer-style learned world models). What is learned from experience here are the belief map and the settings the tuner adopts. That makes this a known-dynamics world model — the same family as classical model-predictive control and the POMDP planners it draws on — which is the right choice when the physics are known and the hard part is deciding, not modeling motion.

How we decide which controller is better

One lucky day proves nothing, so each warehouse type is tested on dozens of matched days, and the average difference is turned into a — a “is this real or just luck?” number. Past +2, we call the self-tuner for that warehouse; near zero we call it flat and keep the simple fixed settings there.

Why races often tie, and what a stress day is

On an ordinary day the fixed settings are already close to right, the tuner correctly changes nothing, and both sides finish identical — a tie is the correct answer, not a glitch. To see the tuner earn its keep, run a : the fleet starts low on battery with a fast-draining pack, charging choices dominate, and the two controllers genuinely part ways. One more safety fact: earlier versions quietly ran pickers until they died mid-shift; the current controller forces any deeply-drained picker to a bay, and both and counts are held at zero.

Wave days vs live-stream days

Most of this page uses wave days: the whole day’s order list is known at the start, like a batch of work handed over each morning. Warehouses also run live streams, where orders appear out of nowhere all day. We tested the self-tuner there too, two ways: forks that imagine only the orders currently visible, and forks that also imagine statistically-plausible future orders. The surprise: the humble version won — imagining plausible futures made the tuner slightly worse, while the visible-only version beat fixed settings by about 1.8% per day, proven across 216 matched days. Even guessing the future responsibly turns out worse than honestly admitting you can’t see it — a pattern this project keeps rediscovering. Use the “live-stream day” checkbox in the Race tab to watch one.

Disturbances & robot senses (M2)

Spills and dropped debris appear at random on the aisles. Robots only know about them by seeing them: each robot senses out to a radius of 5 cells, but racks block the view, so in practice a robot sees down its own aisle and little else. One robot’s sighting becomes the whole fleet’s knowledge, and that knowledge slowly fades. A robot that drives into a spill blind gets stuck spinning its treads until the spill is cleaned. Measured verdict: knowing where debris is only pays when hitting it hurts — and honest eyes capture 28–87% of what a crystal ball would, less the deadlier a single mistake becomes.

Does predicting disturbances actually pay? (measured)

Four fleets ran the same 48 days on a floor with random spills (each spill blocks its cell until dealt with). The only difference is what each fleet knows:

fleetday’s scorerobots that drove into spills
blind (no map)800.6364
sight only (dodge what’s visible, no memory)837.3182
standard (old update rule)821.3236
current map (one look is decisive)850.180
mind-reading oracle (impossible)855.822

Reading the table: honest sensing + the current map earns 90% of everything a mind-reading oracle could add over a blind fleet (+49.5 of +55.3), and cuts spill collisions to a fifth. The “sight only” row splits that gain: dodging what’s currently visible is worth +36.7, and predicting spills outside everyone’s sight radius — believing a spill is still there after the robot walks away — adds +12.8 more and halves the remaining collisions. Eyes do most of the work; prediction does the part no extra eyes could. The jump from the standard map to the current one came from a single fix: a robot’s direct look now replaces what the map believed about that cell instead of casting one vote against a pile of old observations. Same eyes, better memory. The last 5.7 points belong to the oracle alone — spills nobody’s line of sight crosses while they’re down.
